areas.name: Reliable memory, context and skill adaptation for long-running LLM agents
areas.description: Research on how long-running language-model agents preserve, retrieve, compress, validate and update conversational or task experience and reusable procedural skills across episodes and changing environments. The area covers downstream decision quality and evaluation, computational and context costs, temporal validity and applicability, provenance and security, privacy, and interference between historical knowledge or tasks. Its members address related but distinct research problems; membership does not assert that their concrete objectives or failure modes are identical.

members.name: Agent context bloat
members.description: Long software engineering interaction histories inflate computation and latency and distract reasoning, while passive summarization leaves the agent unable to control memory management.

members.name: Agent social re-entry
members.description: Agents in persistent social environments may remember past conversations yet fail to identify when to revisit them, choose to return, or reconstruct enough context for coherent continuation.

members.name: Compression event attribution
members.description: Full-context versus compressed trajectory comparisons are confounded by agent stochasticity and cannot identify which individual compression degrades downstream execution.

members.name: Conversation history beyond context window
members.description: Conversational agents lose older dialogue when context exceeds the window, requiring retrieval or truncation.

members.name: Correction-resistant historical memory
members.description: Same-source record accumulation and persistence after corrections can let historical claims govern current answers.

members.name: Costly memory writes
members.description: Existing agent memory systems use LLMs to organize and consolidate memories, making memory construction costly and slow; compression may also discard surface-level details.

members.name: Coupled skill evolution
members.description: Training selection, use, and distillation separately or with different rewards causes partial or conflicting evolution of an agent skill library.

members.name: Cross-task skill transfer
members.description: Independent-episode agentic reinforcement learning misses reusable patterns between related distinct tasks; multi-stage skill pipelines entangle extraction, retrieval and execution and add overhead.

members.name: Decision-preserving progress compression
members.description: A compressed progress representation may lose information needed to choose between restart and continue even if trace reconstruction looks adequate.

members.name: Decoupled skill evolution and policy optimization
members.description: Fixed meta-skill workflows or separate optimization treat skills as passive and limit their co-adaptation with a reasoning agent.

members.name: Evolving repository-specific skills
members.description: Code structure and conventions change over time; new PRs must update related components coherently and maintain tests, requiring skills to learn from past validated changes.

members.name: Execution instability after context compression
members.description: Recurrent compression may suppress relevant recent interactions, leading to blocked actions and repeated exploration, while effects of individual compactions are poorly understood.

members.name: Generalizable coding skills
members.description: Coding trajectories entangle procedural knowledge with task and repository context, making transfer across diverse coding environments difficult.

members.name: Heterogeneous experience retention
members.description: One global history is expensive and mixes unrelated experiences, while one compressed representation may discard valuable details; future usefulness of experience is unknown.

members.name: Ill-scoped multi-agent adaptation
members.description: Agents in specialized domains need task procedures; unstructured multi-agent evolution lets the backbone decide update scope and can lead to cross-task interference and inconsistent structures.

members.name: Information Entanglement
members.description: Heterogeneous conversational information is mixed into coarse-grained memory units.

members.name: Local memory management
members.description: Memory systems relying on large or API-hosted memory managers prevent private local deployment; it is unclear how small a local model can manage long-term memory.

members.name: Long agent histories
members.description: Growing interaction histories increase inference cost and dilute attention, degrading performance.

members.name: Long-horizon context bloat
members.description: Growing agent histories raise inference memory cost and degrade reasoning through irrelevant information; heuristic or parameter-update compression is brittle or impractical for some models.

members.name: Long-horizon dialogue recall
members.description: Dialogue agents need to recall facts, events, and relationships across interaction histories efficiently.

members.name: Long-lived memory poisoning
members.description: Untrusted stored documents can later steer an LLM agent to an attacker-selected consequential action, such as a payment destination; authorization must survive permitted changes to memory.

members.name: Long-running materials agent workflows
members.description: Materials research spans dispersed knowledge and tools over multi-day studies; agents struggle to extend capabilities, track long tasks, and learn from prior tasks and feedback.

members.name: Lost process information
members.description: Compressed memories can omit historical process details that reduce agent steps.

members.name: Memory Echo
members.description: Repeated retrieval and write-back can multiply positions occupied by a single historical claim, influencing current answers without independent evidence.

members.name: Memory applicability
members.description: Reusing earlier experience without reassessing its relevance can make otherwise solvable code tasks fail.

members.name: Memory governance
members.description: Agentic long-term memory can expose stale, invalidated, cross-scope, contradictory, or failed historical memory as usable context instead of returning useful current context.

members.name: Memory tax
members.description: Reorganizing facts or distilling preferences in a memory process can remove or obscure evidence and degrade performance compared with raw-history retrieval.

members.name: Moving tool capabilities
members.description: As services evolve, familiar tools disappear or change, alternatives emerge, and agents must discover efficient paths and revise accumulated procedural knowledge.

members.name: Net value of agent memory
members.description: It remains unclear whether building dedicated memory improves long-horizon agent performance over direct retrieval from raw history.

members.name: Noise during skill self-evolution
members.description: Errors in learning experience can persist in reusable skills and harm later held-out tasks; existing evaluation emphasizes clean learning or perturbations only after skills are frozen.

members.name: Obsolete fact interference
members.description: An agent can retrieve the newest statement yet answer using an obsolete competing version; combined retrieval and generation scores obscure this failure.

members.name: Organizational Mismatch
members.description: Memory structures built mainly from semantic similarity may miss other associations among conversational information.

members.name: Persistent relational agent memory
members.description: Finite context windows and retrieval-augmented generation pipelines struggle with relational complexity, incremental updates and computational efficiency over long horizons.

members.name: Private personalized cross-user skill evolution
members.description: Isolated user streams lack diversity; sharing raw trajectories harms privacy and a uniform global skill library poorly fits heterogeneous clients.

members.name: Reasoning-history growth
members.description: Long-horizon agents accumulate past reasoning, raising context length and inference cost; deleting it can alter later actions and trajectories.

members.name: Recurrent skill optimization credit assignment
members.description: A skill must improve current rollout quality and revisions must use verified outcomes to improve subsequent skills; model-level updating is costly or unavailable for closed models.

members.name: Reliable agent trajectory compression
members.description: Fixed context budgets constrain long-horizon agents, while heterogeneous observations, reasoning and tool executions require preservation of temporal dependencies, actionable state and structural fidelity; fragmented methods hinder comparison.

members.name: Reliable agent trajectory compression
members.description: Fixed context budgets constrain long-horizon agents, while heterogeneous observations, reasoning and tool executions require preservation of temporal dependencies, actionable state and structural fidelity; fragmented methods hinder comparison.

members.name: Repeated uncertain skill interpretation
members.description: Textual skill documents are repeatedly interpreted and regenerated through LLM reasoning even for previously learned procedures, adding execution uncertainty.

members.name: Restart decision value
members.description: Classification accuracy alone cannot tell whether restarting an agent improves success because replacement opportunity and remaining budget matter.

members.name: Role-aware memory selection
members.description: Relevance-only retrieval overlooks memories that link complementary but semantically weaker information needed to solve a task, and the role of a memory changes across tasks.

members.name: Scientific use validity
members.description: Correctly recalled scientific evidence may be ineligible to support a decision because the outcome or stopping rule was chosen after inspection; retrieval-focused memory tests do not assess this validity.

members.name: Separate long- and short-term memory control
members.description: Finite context windows limit long-horizon reasoning, while separately managed LTM and STM with heuristics or auxiliary controllers limit adaptability and end-to-end optimization.

members.name: Similarity-only memory retrieval
members.description: Standard RAG retrieves memories by semantic similarity alone, overlooking creation time, access frequency, and factual specificity.

members.name: Skill extraction supervision
members.description: Candidate skill text lacks direct supervision for usefulness in actual task solving.

members.name: Skill failure under evolving web environments
members.description: Closed-environment evaluation misses changes to skill invocation context, perception, and execution feasibility encountered during web deployment.

members.name: Skill robustness under web environment evolution
members.description: Learned skills evaluated in closed environments may fail when invocation context, perceptual grounding, or execution feasibility shifts in deployment.

members.name: Snapshot-only memory provenance
members.description: Memory-backed agents need attribution after snapshots leak or migrate when logs, visible outputs, and trusted metadata may be unavailable.

members.name: Sparse rewards for memory actions
members.description: Memory operations induce sparse and discontinuous rewards during training.

members.name: Static test-time policy
members.description: Agents depending on skill or experience retrieval with fixed inference parameters cannot continuously internalize feedback and may accrue context bloat.

members.name: Subtask-aware context for coding agents
members.description: Sequential histories inflate context; trimming without subtask boundaries risks losing unfinished work, while delegating every nested subtask adds execution and coordination overhead.

members.name: Temporal grounding under compression
members.description: Smaller memory extractors may fail to preserve dates needed for temporal reasoning.

members.name: Temporally valid repository memory evaluation
members.description: Existing code-agent benchmarks lack temporally valid histories or control over how relevant earlier tasks are.

members.name: Test-time compression
members.description: Offline-trained compression policies impose collection or training cost and do not adapt to evolving test-time trajectories.

members.name: Undirected skill updates
members.description: Existing skill banks can be updated without direction or verification, and agents are penalized prematurely for failing to use immature skills.

members.name: Unreliable accumulated agent knowledge
members.description: Memories and skills automatically derived from trajectories can carry errors across related tasks and corrupt otherwise useful knowledge without ongoing validation.

members.name: Watermark robustness and utility
members.description: Attribution must withstand memory-lifecycle attacks and retain useful memory behavior without relying on mutable provenance fields.
